3. Data Sources

Observed Data

Coastal flooding trends are based on measurements from permanent tide gauge stations. The original tide gauge data come from the National Water Level Observation Network (NWLON), operated by the Center for Operational Oceanographic Products and Services (CO-OPS) within the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA’s) National Ocean Service (NOS). Daily maximum water levels are derived from the hourly data set maintained by CO-OPS. The analysis was adapted from Sweet et al. (2018).

Projections

Projections also come from NOAA. Sweet et al. (2018) provides a set of NOAA projections of coastal flooding frequency through 2100. These projections, in turn, are based on a set of sea level rise scenarios that NOAA and others published in 2017 (Sweet et al., 2017), which constituted the official U.S. sea level projections feeding into the Fourth National Climate Assessment.

NOAA’s 2017 sea level projections and the associated 2018 coastal flooding projections included six scenarios. The project team selected two of these scenarios at the recommendation of NOAA and because they align most closely to the range of emissions scenarios that the team is using for GCM-based pairings:

  • Intermediate-low, which corresponds to 0.5 meters of global mean sea level rise between 2000 and 2100. The project team has labeled this scenario “lower sea level rise” in the graphics to reduce the chance of it being conflated with the “intermediate” emissions scenario. This scenario can result from emissions scenarios ranging from SSP1-1.9 through SSP3-7.0. Given current sea level observations and estimates of future warming, this scenario provides a reasonable estimate of the lower bound for the most likely sea level rise by 2100.
  • Intermediate, which corresponds to 1 meter of global mean sea level rise between 2000 and 2100. The project team has labeled this scenario “higher sea level rise” in the graphics to reduce the chance of it being conflated with the “intermediate” emissions scenario. This scenario can result from emissions scenarios ranging from SSP2-4.5 through SSP5-8.5. This scenario provides a reasonable upper bound for the most likely range of sea level rise by 2100.

NOAA’s other four scenarios include one lower sea level scenario and three appreciably higher trajectories. The higher sea level rise scenarios represent low-confidence but high-impact possibilities—namely, “tipping points” associated with rapid melt of the Greenland and/or Antarctica ice sheets.

These projections are based on a combination of empirical observations and CMIP5 modeling, but they are not model outputs themselves. Therefore, the project team is referring to them as “projections” or “scenarios,” not “model outputs” as other pairings present.

Note that NOAA published a newer set of scenarios in 2022 (Sweet et al., 2022). The Sea Level pairing uses the newer versions. This coastal flooding analysis does not because the 2022 projections give return intervals and the number of flooding events, but not the number of flood days, which is the metric needed to align with the available observational record. Events can be multi-day. The 2017/2018 scenarios used here are the most recent version with outputs that align readily with EPA’s observed indicator.

4. Data Availability

Observed Data

Individual tide gauge measurements can be accessed through NOAA’s “Tides and Currents” website. This website also presents an interactive map that illustrates sea level trends over different timeframes. The project team obtained 1950–2023 totals from NOAA’s derived product data interface.

Projections

The coastal flooding projections featured here can be downloaded as part of the companion data file to Sweet et al. (2018). The underlying 2017 sea level projections are available from NOAA’s CO-OPS Publications site.
